Senses.Explanation: The Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp is a thirty-fascicle compiled record of Chan teachers and their sayings. Chan authors cite, read, criticize, and identify the book as a documentary source; title occurrences are not assigned to the masters recorded inside it. The cited passages span 6 works and preserve the exact headword in the quoted Chinese. The gloss reports the shared use and leaves each surrounding case to its own recorded exchange.

Senses.Note: The exact headword has 104 occurrences in 28 allowed texts. Most belong to the book title treated in the second sense; the free phrase recurs with being unbroken, continuing the flame, succession, generations, ancestral portraits, and separate teaching regions. Senses.Explanation: To continue the lineage lamps is to carry Chan succession from predecessor to successor and from generation to generation. Yongjue Yuanxian defines the governing lamp image in the Extensive Record of Chan Master Yongjue Yuanxian: successive transmission is compared to a lamp because it breaks darkness and reveals things, and because its illumination can continue without end. His histories then call more than seventy generations an unbroken chain of linked lamps and describe them as linking the lamps while continuing the flame. Hanxiu Ruqian uses the phrase in memorial verses for succession after receiving his predecessor's blows and for two named lineage holders carrying the line in different regions. Zefeng Yue applies it to an ancestral portrait during a teaching-seat address. These uses concern public lineage continuity, not ordinary lamps physically fastened together.

Senses.Explanation: The book Linked-Lamp Essentials is a specific Chan compilation, not the act of continuing a lineage. In his self-preface, Huiweng Wuming says that he selected material from more than six hundred teachers, arranged encounters, questions and answers, comments on old and recent cases, and essential statements under each person's chapter, divided the work into thirty fascicles, and gave it this title. Li Yong's preface says the title was placed on the work and the blocks were carved for circulation. Yongjue Yuanxian later places Wuming's compilation among the five lamp records. A lineage biography records Wuming as its compiler, while Sichong's republication preface calls it the Linked-Lamp Record and recounts its printing history.

Senses.Explanation: ‘Wonderful Guanyin, entering the wild grass with the whole body’ brings a revered figure into rough, ordinary ground. Shiqi Tongyun invokes the line after saying the newborn Buddha's grand gestures disrupt ordinary ground, then asks where the bodhisattva's active work can be found. At a lay patron's request for a child, Feiyin Tongrong uses the image and turns eyes and hands toward a present field of response. At his teacher's memorial, Yingning Zhijing gives the line, lifts his body and stamps the ground. Shanyi Ruchun ends a verse that says the founder's meaning is already plainly told with Guanyin wholly entering the grass.

Senses.Explanation: The good horse moves when it merely sees the whip's shadow: the image makes response precede any actual stroke. In the inherited encounter, an outsider says that Shakyamuni's silence opened his clouded understanding. Asked what the outsider obtained, Shakyamuni compares him to this horse. Yuanwu Keqin, Dahui Zonggao, and Hongzhi Zhengjue each raise that exchange and then append their own judgments. The image is not an unconditional compliment. Yikui Yuankui says that even a good horse moving at the whip's shadow is eight beats late. The comparison therefore names exceptionally prompt response while remaining available for Yikui Yuankui to outstrip.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X78/X78n1553.xml). Tiansheng Expanded Lamp Record. The historical Liangshan Shanji section preserves his verse on Luzu facing the wall. Its opening says that Luzu’s complete command saves the most effort: as soon as he sees a monk arrive, he faces the wall. The continuation speaks of people who know the mind and understand the way recognizing one another without needing raised eyebrows. Liangshan is the voice praising the wall-facing action; Luzu is the teacher being described, and the arriving monk is its occasion. The verse treats recognition without an elaborate exchange as economical. This useful historical witness anchors the later disputes, while its appearance in other lamp recensions remains the same poem rather than another event.
